tests_declared: Flexion-extension cervical radiographs for surgical planning

resident.chief_complaint: Progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, now unable to walk without a walking aid.
resident.history: Fifty-one-year-old delivery man with no significant past medical history presented with progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness over six months, worsening to inability to walk without a walking aid. He also had chronic neck stiffness for over two years and had not sought intervention. He denied any difficulty with hand dexterity, such as using chopsticks, buttoning a shirt, or picking up a coin.
resident.physical_exam: Neurological examination revealed signs of myelopathy in the lower limbs. MRC muscle power grading in both lower limbs (L2-S1) was 4/5. Deep tendon reflexes, including knee jerk and ankle jerk, were exaggerated bilaterally. Babinski's sign was positive bilaterally. The patient had difficulty getting up from an armless chair and was unable to perform tandem gait. No upper limb signs were demonstrated: sensory-motor function and reflexes were normal in both upper limbs, and Hoffman's sign was negative.
key_positive_signs: Exaggerated knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes bilaterally
Difficulty rising from an armless chair
resident.past_history: No significant past medical history. Chronic neck stiffness for over two years, for which he did not seek intervention.
resident.public_message: A 51-year-old man presented with six months of progressive unsteadiness and bilateral lower limb weakness, now requiring a walking aid, and chronic neck stiffness for over two years. Examination showed bilateral lower limb weakness (MRC 4/5), exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, difficulty rising from a chair, and inability to tandem gait; upper limbs were neurologically normal. JOA score was 14/17 (grade 1 disability). Cervical spine X-rays showed degeneration with loss of lordosis and anterior osteophytes C3-C6; CT and MRI showed extensive OPLL from C3 to T3 causing significant canal compromise with no cord signal changes. Diagnosis: extensive cervicothoracic OPLL causing myelopathy.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI were described as showing extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) from C3-T3 with significant canal compromise. No cord signal change was reported. The direction of compression and a graded severity of stenosis were not stated. The described imaging has high correlation with the reported myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy. Bilateral lower limb weakness with exaggerated knee and ankle reflexes, and positive Babinski signs indicate corticospinal tract dysfunction. The absence of upper limb motor, sensory, or reflex abnormalities and a negative Hoffman sign, together with no documented sensory level or sphincter disturbance, means the clinical level cannot be pinpointed to the cervical cord alone; it is compatible with lower cervical or upper thoracic cord involvement. The OPLL from C3 to T3 provides a structural correlate. Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is well recognized in OPLL because the laterally placed lower-limb fibers in the corticospinal tract and the longest axons are most vulnerable to anterior compression. The examination is incomplete as lower limb sensory function, sensory level, and sphincter function are not documented.

red_flags.finding: Normal upper limb motor/sensory/reflexes and negative Hoffman despite OPLL from C3.
red_flags.rationale: Lower-limb-predominant myelopathy is common in OPLL because the lower-limb corticospinal fibers are more laterally placed and more vulnerable to anterior compression, and early disease often spares the upper limbs. This does not offer an alternative cause and does not change the levels already identified by imaging.

red_flags.finding: No cord T2 signal change on MRI.
red_flags.rationale: Absence of T2 hyperintensity does not exclude clinically significant myelopathy, especially in early or dynamic compression. It is not an alternative explanation and does not alter the indication; it may suggest less severe cord damage but does not change the plan.

red_flags.finding: Incomplete documentation of lower limb sensory exam, sensory level, and sphincter function.
red_flags.rationale: The missing data limit precise clinical localization and cannot confirm a sensory level matching the imaged OPLL. However, the upper motor neuron signs already establish a myelopathy above the lumbosacral enlargement, so this gap does not change the diagnosis or the surgical plan.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: There is no fundamental mismatch: the imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise that can explain the bilateral lower limb upper motor neuron syndrome. Notable but non-contradictory observations are the absence of upper limb signs despite C3 involvement and absent cord signal change; both are consistent with early, leg-predominant cervical/thoracic myelopathy. The exact symptomatic level cannot be determined from the examination because lower limb sensory level and sphincter function were not documented.
neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to an upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement, consistent with myelopathy; the absence of upper limb signs means the clinical level is likely lower cervical or upper thoracic, not definitively C3. The imaging shows extensive C3-T3 OPLL with canal compromise, which explains the dominant lower-limb syndrome; the symptom-imaging match is high. Notable findings are all coexisting and do not change the indication or plan: (1) normal upper limbs despite C3 involvement—common in early leg-predominant OPLL; (2) no cord T2 signal—does not exclude myelopathy; (3) incomplete sensory/sphincter documentation—limits precise level but not diagnosis. There is no evidence of coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative MAP target 75 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk moderate. Prone position tolerance moderate. Extubation difficulty unassessable: no airway assessment on record.

preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of lower limb weakness or gait instability, such as new falls or inability to walk even with an aid
Development of new upper limb symptoms, sphincter dysfunction, or a drop in JOA score by 2 or more points
No stabilization or improvement of neurological status after 3 months of structured conservative treatment
Evidence of new or progressive cord signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge that progressive myelopathy carries a risk with delay. However, the absence of cord signal change on MRI and the relatively preserved JOA score (14/17) leave a narrow window for a time-limited, closely monitored conservative trial. A structured program of physical therapy, gait training, activity modification, and serial neurological assessments could be offered for 3-6 months, provided the patient is fully informed and there is immediate access to surgical evaluation if any failure criterion is met. This approach is not without risk, but surgery for extensive OPLL also carries significant morbidity, and early intervention may still be possible if deterioration occurs.

physiatrist_final.public_message: I remain hold. The Deputy Director reiterated the progressive myelopathy and extensive OPLL as strong indications for surgery, but these findings were already part of my risk assessment. I have not been presented with any specific argument that a particular finding in the record — such as the absence of cord signal change or the mild JOA score — should be weighted differently. In my view, the narrow window for a monitored conservative trial remains open, with clear failure criteria and immediate surgical access if deterioration occurs.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has progressive myelopathy from extensive OPLL (C3-T3) with significant canal compromise and no T2 cord signal change. The clinical picture is consistent with cord compression; the lower-limb dominance and preserved upper limbs fit with predominant lower cervical/upper thoracic compression. Surgical decompression is the standard treatment for progressive myelopathy due to OPLL, but the absence of cord signal change and relatively mild JOA score (14/17) raise the question of whether a short period of observation is acceptable. This decision involves balancing the risk of irreversible deterioration with the morbidity of surgery over a long segment.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression (cervical laminectomy/laminoplasty extending over the compressive levels, with possible instrumented fusion) to address the OPLL-related stenosis.
Time-limited conservative management (structured physiotherapy, activity modification, serial neurological assessment) with urgent surgical reassessment if any deterioration.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's suggestion of a 3-6 month conservative trial conflicts with the usual indication for surgery in progressive myelopathy; I am uncertain whether the minimal cord changes and JOA 14 justify this delay.
The optimal extent of decompression (e.g., whether to include thoracic levels and whether fusion is needed) is not clearly defined by the available imaging description.
The lack of upper limb signs despite reported C3 involvement may suggest the main compression is lower; this could affect surgical planning.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed directly to surgical decompression, or is a closely monitored conservative trial acceptable in this specific case?
What surgical approach and extent would you consider most appropriate given the extensive OPLL from C3 to T3?
Do you want additional imaging or specialized input (e.g., a spinal deformity surgeon) before deciding?
vice_opinions.public_message: This is a challenging case: the progressive myelopathy from extensive OPLL strongly suggests surgery, but the mild JOA score and absent cord signal change leave room for debate. I have outlined the main options, but I would appreciate your judgment on the timing and surgical strategy. I defer to your decision.

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated. The patient has progressive myelopathy from extensive OPLL C3-T3 with significant canal compromise. A conservative trial would risk irreversible deterioration. We will proceed with posterior decompressive laminectomy and instrumented fusion from C3 to T3, with intraoperative neuromonitoring, and a contingency for staged anterior decompression if needed.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Posterior decompressive laminectomy C3-T3 with instrumented fusion; intraoperative neuromonitoring (SSEP/MEP); if significant residual anterior compression is present intraoperatively, plan for staged anterior decompression.
delegated_tasks: Resident: schedule surgery, obtain detailed informed consent, arrange preoperative anesthesia evaluation and updated flexion-extension cervical radiographs.
Physiatrist: plan early postoperative rehabilitation and disposition.

director_rulings.public_message: I have reviewed the case and the departmental discussion. The progressive myelopathy with lower limb weakness and imaging showing extensive OPLL C3-T3 with canal compromise warrants surgical decompression now. A conservative trial carries an unacceptable risk of irreversible deterioration. I disagree with the physiatrist's proposed delay. The plan is posterior decompression and fusion from C3 to T3 with neuromonitoring, and a staged anterior approach if needed. We will proceed with surgical preparation and detailed informed consent.
